EDITORIAL—We copy the following notice of the marriage of our young townsman, Edward Drane, Esq, and Miss Rosa Flournoy, of Louisville, from the Courier. May their future be as bright and happy as was their bridal day:

One of the happiest and most pleasant events of the year occurred at the Christian church, corner of Fourth and Walnut streets, at 3 O'Clock yesterday afternoon. It was the marriage of the lovely and accomplished Miss Rosa Flournoy, of this city, Sister of Mrs. Colonel Jilson Johnson, to Mr. Edward Drane, of GAINESVILLE, Tenn, a young gentleman of unexceptionable character and family. DR. Hopson officiated, and the ceremony was beautiful, appropriate, and sensibly brief. Long before the appointed hour a brilliant crowd of friends and relatives assembled in the body of the church, and the scene was to the fair young bride indeed an auspicious welcome to the new life the duties of which she was about to assume. At 3 O'Clock the party entered the church, the bride leaning on the arm of Col. Johnson, who, since the death of her father, has been to her both father and brother. The groom was accompanied by Mrs. Johnson. They met at the altar, in front of which stood DR. Hopson, the pastor of the church, and the ceremony was commenced by a short but earnest and most kind lecture on the duties of their new relation to each other. Kneeling reverently before the minister, the blessing of God was invoked upon their union, and rising they were, by the authority of both Church and state, pronounced man and wife. The newly-wedded pair left immediately for the East, where they will make a tour of the fashionable watering places, and after spending a few weeks in Canada, will return and settle down into a married life, the happiness of which, all who know them sincerely wish may more than justify even their ardent hopes. The bride was the recipient of very many elegant tokens of affection from her friends. Being universally loved for her many charms of mind and person, few of her circle failed to mark their esteem and earnest wishes for her welfare by some tasteful and elegant present. The occasion was an event in Louisville society, which we hope will not be entirely deprived of one of its brightest ornaments.

eign splendors, and art journals that
we liked. On his return he would
make the remark, carelessly enough,
"I met Mr. Vanrogue at the bank
to-day" or "I dined with Mr.
Vogue," or "I declined an invita-
tion to Mrs. Grundy's ball for sweet
sakes."


As a matter of course, two ex-
perienced village girls were ready to
fall down and worship such a hero
in society, and I am not sure but we
looked forward to the day when the
Vogue would open its doors to us, and the
Grundy fiddles do us service. When
I look back upon it I cannot believe
I was in love with Mr. Raoul Rossi-
tur; but there was the charm of the
city in his atmosphere, flavor of
romance in his bearing, added to the
knowledge that half the girls in the
town were courting his favor and re-
ceiving none. Moreover, a young
person is dangerously flattered by
her first lover, and Tom had never
said a soft thing to me in my life,
no matter whatever he may have
thought.


Well, affairs went on after this
manner for some weeks, when I dis-
covered that I was growing jealous
of Ri—jealous if he danced with her
too often, if he leaned over the tall
back of her chair and chatted con-
fidentially. I know there are some
who believe that jealousy is a test
of love, but I was never
jealous of Tom in my life. It's a
test of vanity and self-love, I admit,
and I had a supply of these attrib-
utes in those days, prime quality.
I think Mr. Rossitur must have ob-
served that his attentions to Ri an-
noyed me; for, later he treated her
with perfect civility when in my pre-
sence, but also with entire indiffer-
ence. Now I was fond of Ri. She
might wear my trinkets, my gowns,
my laces, or anything that was mine;
but when it came to my lovers, I
rebelled.


One day the conversation fell upon
jewels, and I wish you could have
heard the fine fancies he had about
them; he was like the girl in the fai-
ry tale who talked pearls and rubies;
so nothing must do but I must show
him my necklace that descended to
me from I don't know how many
great-grandmothers, bless their
hearts! As famous as that necklace
which


"Undine with trembling hand,
Snatched from the wave for Hildebrand"—
It came originally from Venice, had
been presented at court, been ship-
wrecked, and had seen a great deal
of life, no doubt. It is my only heir-
loom.

their own opinion, are wiser than seven men

superior in every respect to everybody. They
have, according to their ideas, superior intel
lectual endowments, and sprung from royal
ancestors, and are by right the heirs to fame.
Young man, whoever you are, that entertain
such notions as these, let me tell you that they
will be your ruin. Nobody will care twenty
years hence who was your father or your
mother. Your saying, or even thinking you
are smart, will not make any one believe it
unless you do something great and wise.
There are great many men covered with in
fanny and shame and clad in rags, who once
were just such boys as you think you are
They were thought by their friends to be re-
markably smart when boys. They were we'll
educated. Many of them graduated in COL
lege with the first honors but to-day they

plies after significant figure in decimals.
It takes up room and nothing more. Rub it
out and the value of the significant figure is
not changed. Add ten thousand ciphers to
such figure and its value is not increased.
Just so with those boys who are wise and
great in their own opinion. They make men
that take up room in this world and nothing
more.

tined to fail, form the other extreme. This
class of boys feel that they are inferior to
everybody else. They are so modest or bash
full, or so destitute of self confidence or some
thing of this kind, that they permit every
body to do just as they please in every res
pect. This class of boys really has more in
tellectual calibre than that spoken of above ;
but there is great defect in one particular.

class has too exalted notions of itself; this
class has an exaggerated notion of its inabili-
ty. The members of the former class think
they are so rich, there is no need to put forth
any effort and the members of the latter class
think they are so poor that it is useless to try.

highest pinnacle of Fame's proud temple; the
latter have no aspirations. Failure awaits
both classes. The young man who overesti-
mates himself is certain to become contempti-

who does not respect himself, never can Sc
cure the respect of others. Ita difficult thing

1t is hard to have proper estimation Of our
selves and not have contempt for others.

The Father OF the Period.

We have heard recently a good deal about the womb of the period and the girl of the period, but so far as we have seen, no one has ever said a word about the father of the period. Whether in the case of the men and women who have addressed us on these interesting subjects they were of the opinion that papa was all right and mamma all wrong or not we do not know; but it looks very much as if they had arrived at that conclusion. So we entirely dissent from that theory. We believe that the fathers of the period are all or nearly all wrong, and that much of what is wicked in the world is to be attributed to these very gentlemen, who have up to this establishment of the newspaper, the pulpit and the lyceum. We have not the space to pursue this subject to the extent that we should like to pursue it and our remarks will therefore be very brief. The father of the period takes as little interest in his children as the wild Comanche Indian in his savage or in his counting-room. The breakfast hour is, as a general thing, a reign of terror to his growing boys. If he condescends to notice them, it is only to growl at them about putting their knives in their mouths and about using their napkins or pocket handkerchiefs. If they are moderately quiet and do not kick each other's shins under the table, and so interfere with his enjoyment of his mutton chop, he is content. All that he wants is peace. Breakfast over he probably condescends to pat the favorite child on the head as he puts his hat on, and then for the balance of the day their care devolves upon their mothers and their teachers, and at four o'clock, when the dinner hour comes, the breakfast routine is again gone through, and he is off to the political meeting, the club-room, or to neighbor Smyth's. The children are put to bed, and he sees no more of them until the inevitable breakfast comes again. We do not think that we have been guilty of any exaggeration in this short sketch, this is the programme for years. It is true that he pays the butchers bill, the tailors and the shoemaker's, and hatters, and that he has done very well when finally he has succeeded in starting them on the road to their own independence in some trade or occupation. In nine cases out of ten boy is indebted to his father for simply this and nothing more. Is it all that he should do? During all these years golden opportunities for cultivation and improvement have been lost. We have good boys around us, the young men that are crowding us on the stage are all that they should do in every respect, it is more the result of pure luck than of the care and attention that they received as a general thing, from their fathers. So much for the father of the period. .....

A Defence OF Pretty Women.

The London Saturday Review, in a recent number prints a gallant defence of pretty women. There are some jealous souls in this world, who always sneer at pretty women and are perpetually reminding us of that horrible old proverb "that handsome is as handsome does," or something to that effect. We have no sympathy or patience with this class of persons. There is nothing in all this world so beautiful as a beautiful woman. It is woman's business and woman's duty to be pretty and beautiful. That she understands this thoroughly without being told of it we well know, for on no other theory can we possibly account for the thousand efforts that she makes to please and to appear attractive. She sometimes overshoots the mark, it is true, and is abused by the very people from whom she had hoped to win. But read what the Review says: After all, is the world so very absurd in its love of pretty women, or woman so very ridiculous in her chase after beauty? A pretty woman is doing a woman's work in the world, not making speeches, nor making pudding, but making life smile and more beautiful. Man has foresworn the pursuit of beauty altogether. John J. Patterson, the senator elect, was arrested at four O'Clock, this evening, in the First National Bank, by Jas. A. A young man had volunteered, and was ex-
pected daily to be ordered to the scat
war. One day his mother gave him an

"Yes," he answered.

The Danbury Negs gives the following free
and easy account of late disaster in that
town:


There was a trifing affair in Branchville on
Friday. Phlos w. Bates has a quarry about
quarter of a mile east of the village. He is
also the owner of blacksmith's shop near
by, where he employs two or three men to
sharpen the tools used in quarrying the stone
for the Sheyaug Road at Bethel In accord
ance with good old New England custom,
the powder used is kept in the blacksmith
shop. There were two kegs partially filed,
and one keg unbroken in the shop at the
time our story opens. 1t was a pleasant day.
There was no bright sunshine, but the gen.
eral appearance Of things out of doors was
mellow and comfortable like. One of the
men was employed at the anvil, hammering
the sultry end of a crowbar. A few grains OF
powder had fallen upon the floor while re-
plenishing the quarry from the open kegs.
We came near forgetting to state this, which
is more important matter than at first
seems probable. The other employees were
busly engaged, as the sons of toll are apt to
be when employed by the day. A balsamic
perfume filled the atmosphere of the shop.


Suddenly fake of streaming hot iron shot
nom the anvil and down among the grains Of
powder which held their slumbering fires to
the floor. There were few unnoticed pops
and flashes, then came hiss, as the fame
shot over into the open kegs. The man who
held the crowbar mechanically passed out
doors. Another son of toll who, with his
back to the danger, was looking through
window, turned around in time to detect one
end of the shop in the act of moving of, fol-
lowed by comrade whose shirt had gone up
in flame. The two partially filed kegs had
exploded with the customary violence, and
the full keg was ON fire. At this juncture
was displayed an act of heroism seldom ex-
hibted in Fairfield County. Mr.. Bates seiz-
ed the burning keg and hurled it out into the
snow, in time to quench the flames, save the
balance Of his shop, and the lives of himself
and men. Two ofthe mem were badly burn
ed, portion of the shop was wrecked, and
two roosters who had been fighting near by
at once buried all animosities engendered by
the fray, and Immediately started over the
hill for home, with the rapid and graceful
gait peculiar to those feathered Mormons.

Conference has held us Celii-Ah and has not done much to interest the "outside" world. Its deliberations were characterized by more liberality of sentiment than any previous session.

Brigham Young prophesied that it was not contrary to the spirit of Mormonism for the "Saints" to send their children to "Gentile" or "Sectarian" schools and have them admitted "free of charge" stating that if the parents were true "Latter Day Saints" the children would not "stray from the fold"—the force of example restraining them from "apostacy."

I wondered what the term or phrase "free of charge" had to do with the subject. The inference to be drawn from it is clear to my mind—if they (the parents) are able to pay for instruction, then send to Mormon schools; otherwise it will not hurt the morals of the innocents to be instructed "free of charge" in "Gentile" or "Sectarian" schools; and it would have the double effect of educating the children and "spoiling the Gentiles" at the same time, as "worldlings" or "outsiders" would denominate that sharp practice.

The 'President' also had a good deal to say or "prophesy" in reference to the "Babylonish fashions of the Sisters, sometimes speaking sarcastically, and at other times descending to vulgarity and almost to obscenity—strangely in keeping with his position—bringing the blush of shame and indignation to many fair cheeks. He says there are many young men who are desirous of marrying and helping to build up the "Kingdom of Heaven" on the earth, but stand appalled at the prospective expense of supporting one or five wives; that it is all a man of moderate means can do to support one when twenty-four yards of material are put in one dress; therefore the Kingdom languishes and is not built up, and the women are to blame for it.

It is a pity about the poor, innocent young men, and the Kingdom also. Both have my sympathies. But, seriously, the "Babylonish fashions" are doing more to break up or do up polygamy than all other forces combined. Make a note of that, ye rebukers of woman's folly and vanity; and while we acknowledge our weaknesses with all humility, allow us poor benighted creatures to take to ourselves the credit of doing something to benefit humanity, if with no other weapon than our love of pretty things, or, as Brother Brigham would term it, our "Babylonish fashions." Wonder if we are out of "our sphere?" But I notice that the venerable prophet, "seer" and "revealer" usually wears the finest of cloth and an elaborate watch and chain, with seal attached, and heavy gold buttons in his sleeves, etc. Now, I have no objection to these articles, and rather admire them; but could not help thinking that by the sacrifice of these "vanities" he might help some brother to wed his thirdly, and thus promote the "kingdom"—but this is from an "outside" standpoint.

Rev. Norman Mcleod is still lecturing on "Polygamy." He also recently delivered two lectures on that dreadful tragedy, the Mountain Meadow Massacre, which, if the main points are true (and he says he can bring proof of all, he affirms), is enough to stir the heart of the Nation to its depths. The picture he drew of murder in cold blood, after sending a flag of truce to induce them to surrender; the violating the women and girls, and then numbering them, is enough to fill with horror any one possessed of a soul. The beautiful tresses of mothers and daughters were taken from their heads for the unhallowed purpose of making a lariat to tie to a horse of one of the murderers, and was used for that purpose for months. He also denounced in scathing terms the vandalism that could destroy the monuments—reared by U. S. officers in memory of the victims—and disintegrate their bones, that loving hands had bundled, and again scatter them on the plains to "blanch in the wastes" as Brigham had predicted.

If Mr. Mcleod intends going east to lecture in Washington when Congress convenes next winter, I have some curiosity to know what impression he will make on our venerable Uncle Sam and his advisers.

Last Saturday morning we were startled and mortified at the announcement of the death, by her own hand, of Mrs. G. Pointer. It is another of those dreadful tragedies that are so often caused by intemperance and its first cousin, domestic infelicity. It is said that her husband was in the practice of indulging in the accursed habit of drinking, and when intoxicated would devote his manly energies to beating his wife; and on that fatal Friday morning he actually kicked and beat her until she bore the marks upon her person. She was rendered perfectly desperate, and evidently intended to make her woe sure, as she used two ounces of laudanum and one of chloroform. Poor, gliding woman how she must have suffered ere she could have resolved to put out the light that no Promethean fires could again relume. Tender hands and a minister administered the last sad rites, and she sleeps at the feet and under the shade of the grand old mountains here.

A MINE ON FIRE.

I was twenty-five years old and was working as regular pitman on the day and night shift, when I fell in love with Mary Andrews, the daughter of one of our head pitmen.

Not that I dared to have told her so, I thought, but somehow the influence of Mary used to lift me up more and more till I should no more have thought of going to join the other pitmen in public house than of trying to fly. It was about this time that I got talking to a young fellow about my age who worked in my shift. John Kelsey his name was, and I used to think it a pity that a fine clever fellow like he was, handsome, stout, and strong, should be so fond of the low habits, dog-fighting, and wrestling, so popular among our men. I was going along one evening past old Andrews' house, when the door opened for a moment as if some one was coming out, but, as if I had been seen, it was closed directly. In that short moment, though, I had heard a laugh, and that laugh surely was John Kelsey's.

Time slipped on, and I could plainly see one thing that troubled me sorely—John was evidently making an outward show of being a hardworking fellow, striving hard for improvement, so as to stand well in old Andrews' eyes, while I knew for a fact that he was as drunken and dissipated as any young fellow that worked in the pit.

I could not tell Andrews this, nor could I tell Mary. If she loved him it would grieve her terribly, and be dishonorable as well, and perhaps he might improve. I can tell him though, I thought, and made up my mind that I would, and meeting him one night, evidently hot and excited with liquor, I spoke to him about it.

"If you truly love that girl, John," I said, "you'll give up this sort of thing."

He called me a meddling fool; said he had watched me; that he knew I had a hankering after her myself, but she only laughed at me; and one way and another so galled me that we fought. I went home that night bruised, sore, and ashamed of my passion while he went to the Andrews' and said he had to thrash me for speaking insulting about Mary.

I heard this afterward, and don't know how it was but I wrote to her telling her it was false, and that I loved her too well ever to have acted so.

Six months passed over my head—six weary, wretched months—till Christmas came on, cold and bitter, but not so cold and bitter as was my heart.

It was Christmas Eve, and in a dreamy listless way I was sitting over my breakfast before starting for work, when I heard a sound, and knew what it meant before there were shrieks in the village, and women running out and making for the pit's mouth, a quarter of a mile away. I tell you I turned sick with horror, for I knew that at least twenty men would be down on the night shift; and though I was close upon their leaving time they could not have come up yet.

"Pit's fired, pit's fired!" I heard people shrieking; not that there was any need, for there wasn't a soul that didn't know it, for the pit had spoken for itself. And as I hurried out I thought all in a flash, oh what a Christmas it would be for some families there, and I seemed to see a long procession of rough coffins going to the churchyard, and to hear the wailings of the widow and fatherless.

I didn't lose any time, you may suppose, in running to the pit's mouth, but those who lived nearer were there long before I arrived. I found that the cage had brought up part of the men, and three who were insensible, and that it was just going down again.

I went down directly and just as it disappeared, who should come running up, pale and scared, but Mary Andrews.

"There's no one belonging to you down there, is there?" asked her.

"Oh, yes—yes, my father was down and John Kelsey as well."

"Now, then, who's going down?" I shouted.

"You can't go down," shouted half a dozen voices, "the choke got most terribly."

"But there are two men down!" I cried savagely. "You're not all cowards, are you?"

Two men stepped forward, and we slid in the cage.

"Who knows where Andrews was?" cried a voice, and a faint voice from one of the injured men told me. Then I gave the warning, and we were lowered down, it having been understood that at the first signal we made were to be drawn up sharply.

We reached the bottom, and I found difficulty in breathing, and, shouting to the men to come on, I ran in the direction where I had been told we should find Andrews; but it was terrible work, for I expected each moment to encounter that deadly gas that had robbed so many men of their lives. But I kept on shouting to those behind me, till at once, tripped, I fell over someone and soon as I could get myself together, lowered the lamp I carried, and to my great delight, found it was Andrews.

Whether dead or alive I could not tell then; but we lifted him among us, and none too soon, for as I took my first step back I reeled, from a curious giddy feeling which came over me.

"Run, if you can," he said faintly, as my legs seemed to be sinking under me. I managed to keep on, though, and at once, the next turn we were in purer air; but I knew it was a race for life, for the heavy gas was rolling after us, ready to quench out our lives if we slackened speed for an instant. We pressed on, though, till I reached the cage, rolled into it, more or less climbed, and were drawn up, to be received with a burst of cheers, Mary throwing her arms round her father's neck, and sobbing bitterly.

"I'm not much hurt," he said, feeling the fresh air reviving him, as he was.

Large sales of imported stock and poultry took place at the Bazaar of Alfred N. Herkness, in Philadelphia. From the Doylestown Intelligencer we clip the following description of the stock and the sale. The animals had been on exhibition for some days before, and were visited by many curious spectators. On the day of the sale the attendance was not as large as on one or two previous occasions of the kind, but the central part of the arena was well filled, and many persons were stationed around the galleries above. A platform, on which the animals were exhibited, and which was also occupied by the auctioneer and quite a number of visitors and reporters, was erected on one side of the circle. Mr. Herkness took prominent position and announced the conditions of the sale—cash before the animals were taken away. The Jersey cows and heifers were first brought on the stand, led by Joseph Moody, the herdsman who had accompanied them from England. The first animal set up was the two year old heifer "GLORIA" which started at $3.50 and was knocked off at $3.50 to N. B. Brown of Pittsburgh. The next, also a two-year heifer, was sold at $160 to Mr. Cook, of Foxborough Massachusetts. These prices were a fair index of the whole. The third was sold at $3.50; the fourth at $270, and her calf, only a few days old, at $40; the fifth at $160; the sixth at $3.50; the seventh, a bronze gray heifer, to calve in November, 1910; the eighth, three-year old cow, in the same condition, $110; the ninth at $210, to Robert H. Sayre, of Bethlehem; the tenth at $3.50; the eleventh at $500, and her calf at $75; the twelfth, very handsome three year old, at $3.50 to Mr. Cook, of Massachusetts, and the thirteenth, five year old cow, at $270 to the same gentleman. A Jersey bull, 18 months old, was then brought out. The bidding on him was not very lively, and he was struck off at $3.50 to Mr. Cook who was a large purchaser. Five nursery heifers, each two year old, were then in succession brought off the stage. The first sold at $110; the second at $500; the third at $170, and her calf at $685; the fourth, which has been sick during the voyage, at $65 and the 5th at $3.50, to Thomas N. Harvey, of West Grove, Chester County, who is a frequent purchaser of imported stock. Two fine Hampshire Down rams were sold at $40 and $37 respectively, to Middletown, Pa. Two yearling ewes of the same breed brought $32 and $3.50. Two Cotswold rams brought $50 each, and two ewes at $50 each—all purchased by Amos H. Kapp, of Northumberland. There were certainly bargains in these sheep. A very fine Devon Bull, now three years old, bred in Ireland by a gentleman who had secured several prizes with him, was bought by a butcher named McFilan, at $780. This animal was in very fine condition, and weighed on the scales 191 pounds; he was invoiced at the Gus Tom-house at $3.50 in gold, and his transportation cost a large additional sum. It was shame to see this splendid breeding animal struck off to the butcher at beef price, or less. Four Welsh ponies were sold—very nice and graceful animals, but quite unbroken. They brought $145, $140, $110 and $50 respectively. One or two of them were worth more money, but the prevalent horse disease doubtless lessened their market value. Five trios of dark Brahma fowls, of premium strains, were sold at prices from $11 to $12 each; three trios of buff Cochin brought $16 each and one trio of Pencilled Hamburgs brought $15. Pigeons were sold at from 50c to &c per pair. The sale closed by disposing of a dozen or more small terrier dogs, which were arranged on board beside the auctioneer and excited a great deal of fun. The first dog offered brought $40, but several others ran up to $50 and $50. A pair of bull terriers brought $3.50. The duties of the auctioneer were admirably performed by Mr. Herkness, who worked hard to obtain satisfactory prices for the stock. The horned cattle brought pretty fair figures, except the Devon bull, which was certainly sacrificed. The sheep sold comparatively low and the same was the case with several of the ponies. The fowls and dogs brought about their full value. On the whole the venture was probably not a very profitable one to Mr. Fowler, the exporter, on whose account the sale was made.

Gradually we here in Richmond are getting the liberty to leave Richmond—to get out into the rural, producing districts, with which we have natural sympathies; and with which we should have an intimate and cornwardly, southwardly, and westwardly. We have seen the first steps towards our liberation northwardly, also southwardly, and the day is not distant when we shall have Richmond road to Lynchburg and beyond in the Southwest, as well as the Chesapeake and Ohio to the valley of the Mississippi.


There is every now and then a new sign of encouragement with reference to our prospects in all these directions. Southwardly the Chinese wall of Petersburg was broken down not long ago, after years of labor to make an opening through it. But still there is the want of something—we cannot exactly say what—to make the connections through Petersburg with North Carolina efficient, for the fair participation of Richmond in the business of that part of the world. Whatever the immediate difficulty, it would be promptly removed by close connection and practical and wise tariffs between the roads running in that direction. That such connection will be established we do not doubt, and it will probably be facilitated by circumstances just in course of combination. The most important is the removal of the president of the Petersburg and Weldon railroad REUBEN RAGLAND, Esq., from Petersburg to this city. That gentleman will be quite an acquisition to us as a man of wealth, great energy, and sagacity. He is a man of modern views. In commerce, industry, and improvements he is quite up to the spirit and policy of the day, and we anticipate that we shall in due time find this out to the advantage of Richmond.


The intelligent and enterprising gentleman who governs the Wilmington and Weldon railroad has a modern stamp in his opinions and in his commendable and progressive energies. He has an exalted opinion of the prospects and resources of this city, and has for years endeavored to open trade with her that would be alike beneficial to his road and to Richmond. Nothing that he can do to facilitate our trade with North Carolina will be left undone.

ing his destination. We are glad to
state the little fellow is again under
the parental eye.

Mr. EDITOR—The sudden and unexpected death of the Hon. George Coffing, at his home in Salisbury, on the 21st of Nov, has produced profound and painful sensation, not only in the immediate vicinity of his home, but in a wider circle and with larger number of his fellow men than often falls to the lot of an untitled business man. Seeking no public employment, but rather preferring the grateful walks of private life, and an unostentatious devotion to his own affairs, he would nevertheless claim the title of Honorable by virtue of offices bestowed upon him by his fellow citizens, having been member of both houses of the General Assembly of the State. This title, however, was more significant in the minds of his fellow men as indicative of honorable dealing, rather than of public position.

Mr. Coffing was born in Salisbury, in May, 1822, and having never had any other permanent home than that in which he died, on the paternal estate, his life has proved an exception to the maxim that a prophet is not without honor, save in his own country, for he was always honored and respected, and most by those who knew him best. He received creditable academical education, and without exhibiting any peculiar adaptation to a business life, aided his father in the early years of his manhood in the care of his extended business. Upon the decease of his father he gave a few years to the manly and vigorous prosecution of agricultural pursuits, and in the cultivation of his farm and the raising of fine stock, set an example worthy of imitation by the farmers around him. In his enlarged intercourse with his fellow men, his capacities for business were rapidly and largely increased, and he soon felt that the moderate fortune which he had inherited, could be made available in a wider field of operation. At the age of 26 or 27 he engaged with his brother, John H. Coffing, Esq, in the manufacture of iron, in Berkshire county, Mass. where the foundations of an extensive business had been laid by the late firm of Hooley & Coffing of Salisbury. This association with his brother continued for several years when the latter withdrew from the business, and left increased cares upon the subject of this notice. He found himself adequate to the discharge of these added responsibilities however, and there was no interruption to the business. How he enlarged this field of operations may now be seen in the successful working at his decease, of six or seven blast furnaces, with 1 in Connecticut and Massachusetts, under his supervision, as well as the care of numerous iron mines, and works for still other manufactures. An added business achievement, however, was accomplished under his direction, in the erection and management of car wheel establishment at Ramapo, in the state of New York, which is now in successful operation and believed to be the largest in the Union. As a proof of his business capacity and energy, his agent at this latter establishment in one month stated that the orders for wheels were accommodating far beyond their capacity to execute in any reasonable time, and inquired what he should do with them. The prompt and laconic reply was "Receive all the orders and I will relieve you." Within very brief period, men and materials were collected and Mr. Coffing appeared at his works with them, and very soon the capacity of the establishment was doubled and customers were supplied. Not two weeks before his decease Mr. Coffing was elected president of another similar company, just about to commence operations in the state of New York, where his energy, capacity, and wise counsels will be greatly missed, as they will be in all the departments in which they were engaged. The proceeding statement though brief, witnesses amply to his business capacity. Socially, he was in all respects gentleman. As a citizen he was faithful in the discharge of all his duties, and his liberality is testified to in all the public improvements in the town requiring his aid. In regard to his domestic relations as husband, father, friend and employer, it is only necessary to say that such households as his were the charm of domestic life, and if they were multiplied there would be less occasion for the frustration of such associations as tend too often to the arrangement of otherwise happy homes.

The community deplores an honorable life, terminated too briefly according to human view, and apparently in the midst of its greatest usefulness.

language can depict, make altogether a scene
which the word lovely, hackneyed though it

The valley leading from Greenfield to the
Hoosac tunnel, on the other hand, is one con-
tinuous line of wild, rugged, romantic scenery.

which the rough, jagged mountains often pre-
cipitously rise, or lofty hills smoothly clad in

circumstance attending its junction with the
latter river. Just below the town of Greenfield

confluence the Deerfield flows NORTH while the

geology, says there is only one similar instance

magnificent prospect of the valley below, where

read Mr. Hall made the following remarks:

extremes in the administration of the Fed-
eral Government; and,

Though why it is so, we can't tell, of course
But true it is, Messieurs—the public servants
Your laws are honored more in breach than in

observance.
Some time ago we think we can recall
The passing of an ordinance, for all
The houses of our city to be numbered;
But evidently somebody has numbered.
For up to date—despite the will expressed
of those who always do things for the best
The most of dwellings, both the small and

BIGGER,

Are minus any kind or sort of figure.
Now will our worthy Council quit their slum-

bers,

And give their prompt attention to the num-

bers?
Moreover, while upon these interesting themes,
We ask, why quiet peoples rest and dream
Should be disturbed by roaming up and down
of noisy, drunken loafers through the town.
It's hoped the policeman will not hurl his

stick at us

But we do wish and want him more ubiquitous.
In this connection, let us further state
That many of us solemn protest make
Against the license—for a paltry dole
of even ONE additional BEER HOLE.
None will assert that any good can come
From ale or beer, gin, whiskey, or from rum.
The state of morals now is low enough,
Away with all the vendors of this stuff!
The corners of our streets, too, are infested,
Taken possession of, usurped, invested
by gangs of loafers, low, profane and vicious
We cannot help but feel at times suspicious.

As far as possible from these retreats
Of idle loungers blocking up the way,
Annoying peaceful people night and day.
Remonstrance and complaint seem all in vain,
The nuisance still continues just the same.
Ye worthy guardians of the public peace
Ye valorous, courageous night police!
Pray help us in this matter which so vexes us,
And start these loafers quickly on their exodus.
Concerning other things, much might be said,
But "half loaf is better than no bread."
And so, if these few things can be redressed,
We then can give attention to the rest.
With all due deference we present this plea
To be considered by the "powers that be;"
And hope our suit will not prove all in vain,
Although delivered in rhyming strain.
The laws are good—of course, we want no

better,

But please enforce them to the letter;
Treat all alike, and favor show to none,
And then the purpose aimed at will be won.
We may not reach very high renown,
But this will be an orderly and well kept town.
We vote for each of you to keep his place,
And do your bidding with right good grace;
That we have thus spoke for the many, we

believe,

And having had our say, we take our leave.

Some name to this we must append,
For so the Editors do all contend,
"Or else it won't appear," then we should cry,
And so we humbly sign ourselves

SKY-HIGH.

His Grace Archbishop Perret
came to the church, preceded by the religious
societies in the following order: Boys of the
Angels Society, numbering forty-nine, all
bearing beautiful banners; Children, say
about sixty, all wearing white dresses; Lad
Happy Death Confraternity, with the image
of Our Lady Of Seven Sorrows; St. Vincent's
Section of the Catholic Militant Union, with
cross numbering sixty eight members, wearing
badges of St. Vincent de Paul and silver
crosses, and carrying magnificent banners
representing the patron of the church. All the
children to be confirmed followed His Grace.
At his entrance into the church, after the
usual economics on such occasions, His Grace
was addressed in the following words by Rev.
Father Foltier, pastor:
"Allow me, Most Rev. Archbishop, to express,
in my name and in that of the faithful, behold—
You in this very church on which His
Grace, one year ago, invoked the blessings of
the Lord. We are by no means rich in the things of this
world, but we have been blessed in His mercy,
noted over the Catholics of Louisiana so as
to distinguish a prelate such as you are before
God and by man; and in your sound administration,
they, acknowledging the steady progress of the Catholic cause,
praise your virtues, zeal and success.
For while, in this congregation, we see illustriously
on the one hand, Creoles sprung from that
nation of France where the souls have
always been devoted to their consecration,
and from whence souls have established
the Kingdoms of God in the remotest
parts of the world; on the other hand,
we have Irishmen from time to time, who
once belonged to the Emerald Isle, which
was ever renowned for its attachment to its
faith, as well for its patience to and endurance
of prosecutions which made it a nation of martyrs, never faltering, never
wavering, workers of Providence, they are
destined to build up Catholic churches in all.
Between the people of these nations, for
they are by the same baptism and in the same
faith, there must be one feeling of unity.
The feelings of nationality, they agree to
His Grace's will, which has assigned St. Vincent de
Paul the parish church of this altar. Prompted by the same sentiment,
her gratitude and love towards your Grace,
we beg God to bless this day and the
advancement of the Catholic cause."
His Grace answered this address with
the usual eloquence and felicity of expression.
He said he was glad to see both Irish and
French, in spite of the difference of language,
just uniting at the same altar; this was the Catholic
spirit which united all nations and all
peoples in the bosom of Our Holy Church.
He was glad to see that fine church and
the contented congregation, the building of the one and
the other being a collection and harmonious working of
one to the other, which some had thought impossible,
is now an accomplished fact. It is true that
the Rev. Pastor has incurred heavy debts,
but he relies upon the good will, already manifested
by his congregation, to assist him in paying
them, and he will not be disappointed.
After the "Veni Creator" had been sung,
His Grace addressed those who were to be
confirmed, speaking chiefly of the spirit of
fortitude so necessary in our times. He then
confirmed 1876 persons, of whom three hundred
are adults, six of the latter being converts.
At 2 o'clock the ceremonies ended and
His Grace was escorted back to the parochial
residence by the Societies which had attended,
and afterwards dispersed.

shown that phosphorus is so readily
absorbed by carbon that, taken in the
form of pills, carbon constitutes complete antidote. The pills are made of
animal charcoal, powdered and mixed
with little gum. In match factories

use.

HOOP.—On Monday, February 25, 1879, at his
residence near Hull Prairie, JAMES HOOP, in
the sixty fifth year of his age.

The deceased was a native of Scotland, but
came to the Maumee Valley in 1854, where he
has continued to reside until the period of his
death. In 1857 he entered into business rela-
tions with his brother WILLIAM, in Perrysburg,
in which he continued until their removal to
Bowling Green, when he retired from active bu-
siness life, and on two occasions since then he
visited the home of his youth and the friendly
associates of his earlier days.

The deceased was a gentleman who possessed
an extensive acquaintance with men and things,
in fact there was scarcely a subject for discuss-
ion but which he could converse fluently re-
garding it, so general had been his reading, his
habits of study and powers of observation.
His ready address, genial manners and friend-
ly personality commanded the respect of all with
whom he associated and his death will leave a
blank place in the large friendly circle of which
he filled an important part.

with the highest standard of personal rectitude;
he was a frank, candid and honest man, one of
those whose death is always a loss to the com-
munity.

REV. G. A. ADAMS, at Hull Prairie on the 25th
inst. after which, all that was mortal of our de-
ceased friend was interred at Bowling Green, a
large number of sympathising friends being in
attendance.

The ancient geographers used to affirm

whirlpool, of past dimensions, and OF

Of its circle that the mariner, who came
within its influence, was unaware of is
existence. He fancicd that his course
scarcely deviated from right line, and
was delighted with the ease Of the navi-
cation, and the rapidity Of his progress.
Warning voices were lifted, but they were
scoifed at, and ridculed Swifter and
yet swifter went the doomed vessel mar
rover and yet narrower grew the multi
plying circles; stronger and yet stronger
the power that drew him to the terrible
vortex, until at last, escape was impossible,
and hope of rescue forever fed amid re-
volving wrecks, and ghastly corpses, and
ruined argosies with the shrek Of despair
bursting from his lips, he went down to
his ocean grave, with the seaweed for his
winding sheet, and the hoarse winds of
heaven to sing his requiem song; the
victim Of confidence in his own safety, in
his own power of escape from the dangers
into which he needlessly ventured.


What is called the moderate use Of in :
toxicating drinks, is moral maelstrom.
He who ventures within the circle of Its
power, goes there confident of safety, and
sure that he can securely navigate these
dangerous seas. The sun shines in bright
ness above him, and the breezes blow in
in quiet softness around him. On, and
onward yet he glides; stronger aud yet
stronger are the currents which bear him
to his ruin. Warnings are unheeded and
apprehonsions of danger are turned to
ridicule. The whirpoo, gathers and bois
around him. Alarm rises within him.
Hope deserts him. Escape is no longer
among the possibilities of his being, and
at last with wailings Of agony bursting
from his lips, while the wrecks of human
hopes, and human hearts are all around
him, he goes to the perditon of ungodly
men, and creation bows itself in sadness
and wells itself in mourning while it cele-
brates the obsequies of a lost soul.


Let us then settle it in our minds for
ever that even the moderate use of intox
icating drinks is full Of danger. Over
the portals that furnish entrance to this
pathway, ought to be posted in legible
chacters, so plain that he who runs may
| III
who enters here does it at his peril. 1t is
a downward path, and to nothing may we
more appropriately apply the words of

prove her pet delusion, the youthful doctor said,
after a well-timed pause:

"Madame, the frog is there, but I will re-
move it."

He then prescribed an innocent emetic, and
went to the nearest flower shop, where he
bought a small green frog. Armed with this
confederate he presented himself once more
before the duchess, and placed a large basin of
water in readiness. The emetic began to take
effect, the duchess' eyes filled with tears, and
our doctor took advantage of the opportunity
to slip the green frog into the basin.

On seeing the frog a load was removed from
the duchess' heart and for an instant all
seemed well. The next moment she turned
pale, and, as Dr. Cabarus supported her tot-
tering frame she cried, in a despairing tone:

"Oh, doctor! I am not yet cured, for the
frog has left little ones behind her!"

"Stop!" cried Cabarus, without allowing
a trace of embarrassment to be seen in his
manner; "that we shall soon see."

He then threw a searching glance upon the
frog, which he had by this time taken in his
hand, and uttered with certainty that settled
the whole question, these words:

"Madame, that is an impossibility, for the
frog is male."
